common_name: Mrs. Dudley Cross Rose (Antique Cream-Blush Tea Rose)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Mrs. Dudley Cross is a vigorous antique Tea rose that tolerates Gulf Coast heat and humidity with minimal winter protection in zone 7-9.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Mrs. Dudley Cross is a classic Tea rose bearing pale yellow buds that open to soft cream flowers gently blushed with pink, produced in flushes almost continuously through the long, hot Gulf South growing season. Like other old Tea roses it is exceptionally vigorous, heat-tolerant, and disease-resistant, thriving with little more than a sunny, well-drained spot and occasional shaping, which has kept it in circulation among heirloom rose collectors and found growing untended at old homesites for generations. Prune lightly after each bloom flush to encourage continued repeat flowering, and expect good resistance to black spot and powdery mildew compared with modern hybrid roses bred for cooler climates.

common_name: Maman Cochet Rose (Large-Flowered Antique Tea Rose)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Maman Cochet, introduced in 1893, is one of the most widely grown Tea roses across the old Deep South, valued for large, high-centered blooms and strong heat tolerance.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Maman Cochet, introduced in 1893, produces large, full, high-centered flowers in soft pink shaded with cream on the reverse of the petals, opening from long, elegant buds that made it a favorite cut flower and exhibition rose in its era. It remains one of the most widely planted and beloved Tea roses in old Southern gardens for its combination of exceptional bloom size, repeat flowering through the growing season, and the toughness and heat tolerance characteristic of Tea roses. Prune lightly after each flush to encourage continued rebloom, and expect strong resistance to black spot and powdery mildew even in humid Gulf Coast summers.

common_name: Perle des Jardins Rose (Fragrant Creamy-Yellow Antique Tea Rose)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Perle des Jardins, a French Tea rose introduced in 1874, was historically valued as a florist's rose for its fragrant, pale creamy-yellow blooms.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Perle des Jardins, introduced in France in 1874, bears full, richly fragrant, pale creamy-yellow flowers that were prized historically as a cut flower and greenhouse florist rose before becoming a mainstay of heirloom garden collections. Like other Tea roses it repeats reliably through the growing season and tolerates heat and humidity with far less disease pressure than many modern hybrid teas, needing only a sunny, well-drained spot and occasional light pruning after each bloom flush. Its soft yellow color and strong fragrance make it a distinctive addition to an antique rose collection or mixed border.

common_name: Madame Joseph Schwartz Rose (Ivory-Blush Sport of Duchesse de Brabant)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Madame Joseph Schwartz, introduced in 1871, is a white-blush sport of the classic Tea rose Duchesse de Brabant and shares its toughness and rebloom in Gulf Coast heat.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Madame Joseph Schwartz, introduced in 1871, is an ivory-white Tea rose blushed with soft pink that arose as a sport of the classic Duchesse de Brabant, sharing its parent's cupped, informal flower form, rich fragrance, and outstanding heat tolerance. Long grown as a 'found rose' in old Texas and Deep South gardens, it blooms in flushes almost continuously through the growing season and requires little care beyond a sunny, well-drained site and occasional light pruning after each flush. Its excellent disease resistance and easygoing nature have kept it a favorite in heirloom rose collections for generations.

common_name: Blush Noisette Rose (The Founding Noisette Rose)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Blush Noisette is the founding rose of the Noisette class, bred in Charleston, South Carolina in the early 1810s and one of the very few rose classes to originate in North America.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light afternoon shade. Blush Noisette is historically significant as the original rose of the Noisette class, raised from seed in Charleston, South Carolina around 1811-1817 by rice planter John Champneys and further developed by nurseryman Philippe Noisette, making it one of the very few major rose classes bred in North America. It produces large clusters of small, soft pink, sweetly fragrant blooms in nearly continuous flushes through the growing season, on a vigorous, arching shrub that can be grown as a large shrub or trained as a modest climber. Noisette roses remain some of the best-adapted roses for the heat and humidity of the Deep South, and Blush Noisette needs little more than a sunny site and occasional shaping to perform for decades.

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, with a sturdy trellis, arbor, or fence to support the climbing canes; Lamarque is a vigorous 1830 Noisette climber well adapted to Gulf Coast heat and humidity.

directions: Plant at the base of a sturdy trellis, arbor, or fence in well-drained soil in full sun, tying in the vigorous climbing canes as they grow. Lamarque, introduced in 1830, is a classic climbing Noisette rose bearing large, creamy-white, lemon-scented blooms in generous clusters, repeating through the growing season on a vigorous plant that can climb 15 to 20 feet or more where conditions favor it. Like other Noisettes it was bred for the heat and humidity of the American South and remains one of the best-performing large climbers for that climate, tolerating the disease pressure that limits many modern climbing roses. Train canes horizontally along a support to encourage the most flowering laterals, and prune lightly after the main flush to maintain shape and promote continued rebloom.
